lead: A continuous-time Markov chain moves at random times, not on a fixed clock. After entering a state it waits for an exponential sojourn, then jumps to another state. The memoryless exponential keeps the future dependent only on the present state. Engineers use it for queues, call centres, machine failure and repair, and chemical reaction networks. Rates, not probabilities, describe the motion, so the generator matrix replaces the discrete transition matrix.
prereq: You need discrete-time chains for the jump chain and Unit 3, the exponential distribution for sojourn times.

blocks.text: Let {X(t): t ≥ 0} be a random process with a countable state space S. It is a continuous-time Markov chain (CTMC) when, for every state j and every history up to time s, P(X(t+s)=j | X(u), 0≤u≤s) = P(X(t+s)=j | X(s)). The future depends on the past only through the present state. The general name is a Markov process; a CTMC is the countable-state case.

After the chain enters state i, it stays there for a random sojourn T_i, then jumps. In a CTMC, T_i is exponential with rate λ_i > 0: P(T_i > t)=e<sup>−λ_i t</sup> and E[T_i]=1/λ_i. The exponential is memoryless (Unit 3), so however long the chain has already waited in i, the remaining wait has the same distribution. That property makes the Markov description valid at every instant.
Transition probabilities are P_ij(t)=P(X(t)=j | X(0)=i), the chance of being in j after t time units given a start in i. Collect them in the matrix P(t). Then P(0)=I, the identity.

blocks.where: P_ij(t) is the transition probability from state i to state j in t time units; P(t) is the matrix of these probabilities; I is the identity matrix.

sections.h3: Generator Q and the jump chain

blocks.text: Rates replace one-step probabilities. For i≠j, q_ij ≥ 0 is the rate of jumps from i to j, with unit 1/time. Some syllabi call Q the infinitesimal generator or rate matrix. The diagonal entry is q_ii = −Σ_{j≠i} q_ij. Thus every row of Q sums to 0, and q_ii ≤ 0.

The total rate out of state i is λ_i = −q_ii. The sojourn time in i is exponential with rate λ_i and mean 1/λ_i. On a jump from i, the next state is j with probability p_ij = q_ij / (−q_ii) for j≠i, and p_ii=0. The discrete chain with these p_ij is the jump chain: it records where the chain goes, not when.

blocks.where: q_ij for i≠j is the jump rate from i to j; q_ii is the negative total exit rate; p_ij is the probability that the jump chain goes from i to j.

blocks.text: Figure values: q_01=2 per hour and q_10=3 per hour. Then q_00=−2, q_11=−3, and Q = [[−2, 2], [3, −3]]. The jump chain has p_01=1 and p_10=1 because each state has only one exit.

Kolmogorov equations tie P(t) to Q. The forward equations are P′(t)=P(t)Q, and the backward equations are P′(t)=QP(t), with P(0)=I. In entries, P′_ij(t)=Σ_k P_ik(t) q_kj for the forward form. For a finite state space these equations give all transition probabilities from the rates.

A stationary distribution π is a probability vector with πQ=0 and Σ_i π_i=1. It gives the long-run fraction of time in each state when the chain is irreducible and positive recurrent. Do not confuse π with a row of P(t). The stationary distribution of the jump chain generally differs because the CTMC spends longer in slowly exited states.

blocks.where: π is the stationary row vector; π_i is the long-run fraction of time in state i; Q is the generator.

blocks.text: Birth–death process: states 0,1,2,...; from n the chain goes to n+1 at rate λ_n or to n−1 at rate μ_n (μ_0=0). Its generator has q_n,n+1=λ_n, q_n,n−1=μ_n, and q_nn=−(λ_n+μ_n). A Poisson process is the pure-birth case μ_n=0 and λ_n=λ: counts rise by one at rate λ and never fall. See 7.3.

figure.caption: Rate diagram: the chain jumps 0→1 at rate 2 per hour and 1→0 at rate 3 per hour; no self-loop is drawn because self-jumps are not part of the jump chain.

spec.aria: A two-state rate diagram shows a jump from state 0 to state 1 at rate 2 per hour and back at rate 3 per hour.

examples.question: A two-state CTMC has jump rate 2 per hour from state 0 to state 1 and 3 per hour from state 1 to state 0. (a) Write Q. (b) Find the stationary distribution. (c) Find the mean sojourn time in each state in hours and minutes.
steps: Rate out of state 0 is 2 per hour, so q_00 = −2 and q_01 = 2.
Rate out of state 1 is 3 per hour, so q_11 = −3 and q_10 = 3. Thus Q = [[−2, 2], [3, −3]].
Stationary equations πQ=0 give −2π0 + 3π1 = 0 and 2π0 − 3π1 = 0, which are the same. So 2π0 = 3π1.
Mean sojourn in state 0: 1/2 h = 0.5 h = 30 min. Mean sojourn in state 1: 1/3 h = 0.3333... h ≈ 20 min.
examples.answer: Q = [[−2, 2], [3, −3]], π = (0.6, 0.4), mean sojourns 0.5 h (30 min) in state 0 and 1/3 h ≈ 0.3333 h (20 min) in state 1.

pi1 = q01 / (q01 + q10)

traps: Q row sums are zero, not one. The off-diagonal rates in a row add to −q_ii, not to 1.
Off-diagonal q_ij are rates, so they can exceed 1 and carry unit 1/time. They are not probabilities.
q_ii is negative, or zero for an absorbing state. Forgetting the sign gives a negative mean sojourn time.
Mean sojourn in state i is 1/(−q_ii), using the total exit rate. It is not 1/q_ij for one chosen exit j.
The stationary distribution solves πQ=0 with Σπ_i=1. Do not normalise Q rows or use the discrete-time equation π=πP.

quiz.q: What is the row-sum property of the generator Q of a CTMC?
quiz.a: Every row sums to 0: q_ii = −Σ_{j≠i} q_ij.

quiz.q: What distribution does the sojourn time in state i follow, and what is its mean?
quiz.a: It is exponential with rate −q_ii; its mean is 1/(−q_ii).

quiz.q: Why does an exponential sojourn make the CTMC Markov?
quiz.a: The exponential is memoryless. Given that the chain has already waited t in a state, the remaining wait has the same exponential distribution, so the past waiting time does not change future jump probabilities.

quiz.q: A two-state CTMC has rate 4 per hour from state 0 to state 1 and rate 1 per hour from state 1 to state 0. Write Q and the mean sojourn times.
quiz.a: Q = [[−4, 4], [1, −1]]. Mean sojourn in state 0 = 1/4 h = 0.25 h = 15 min. Mean sojourn in state 1 = 1/1 h = 1 h = 60 min.

quiz.q: For the rates 4 per hour from 0 to 1 and 1 per hour from 1 to 0, find the stationary distribution.
quiz.a: Solve πQ=0 with Q = [[−4, 4], [1, −1]]. The equation gives 4π0 = π1. With π0 + π1 = 1, π0 = 1/5 = 0.2 and π1 = 4/5 = 0.8.

quiz.q: A student writes q_12 = 3 and q_11 = −3, and also q_13 = 2. What is wrong?
quiz.a: If q_11 = −3, the total exit rate from state 1 is 3. Then q_12 + q_13 must equal 3. With q_12 = 3, q_13 must be 0, so q_13 = 2 is impossible.

quiz.q: Why can an off-diagonal q_ij be 10 per hour while a discrete transition probability must be at most 1?
quiz.a: q_ij is a rate, not a probability. Over a small time h, the jump probability is about q_ij h. For a small enough h, q_ij h ≤ 1, so a large rate is allowed.

beyond: Not for the exam. Continuous-time Markov chains model queue lengths in call centres, machine up/down states in reliability, and chemical reactions in systems biology. The same generator appears in Markov chain Monte Carlo and in performance models of computer and communication systems. Search for birth–death processes, queueing theory, M/M/1, generator matrix, and Kolmogorov equations.
